gallery.title: File:Earth-moon.jpg
gallery.description: This view of the rising Earth greeted the Apollo 8 astronauts as they came from behind the Moon after the fourth nearside orbit. Earth is about five degrees above the horizon in the photo. The unnamed surface features in the foreground are near the eastern limb of the Moon as viewed from Earth. The lunar horizon is approximately 780 kilometers from the spacecraft. Width of the photographed area at the horizon is about 175 kilometers. On the Earth 240,000 miles away, the sunset terminator bisects Africa.

gallery.title: File:Crab Nebula.jpg
gallery.artist: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University)
gallery.description:
This is a mosaic image, one of the largest ever taken by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, of the Crab Nebula, a six-light-year-wide expanding remnant of a star's supernova explosion. Japanese and Chinese astronomers recorded this violent event in 1054 CE.
The orange filaments are the tattered remains of the star and consist mostly of hydrogen. The rapidly spinning neutron star embedded in the center of the nebula is the dynamo powering the nebula's eerie interior bluish glow. The blue light comes from electrons whirling at nearly the speed of light around magnetic field lines from the neutron star. The neutron star, like a lighthouse, ejects twin beams of radiation that appear to pulse 30 times a second due to the neutron star's rotation. A neutron star is the crushed ultra-dense core of the exploded star.
The Crab Nebula derived its name from its appearance in a drawing made by Irish astronomer Lord Rosse in 1844, using a 36-inch telescope. When viewed by Hubble, as well as by large ground-based telescopes such as the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, the Crab Nebula takes on a more detailed appearance that yields clues into the spectacular demise of a star, 6,500 light-years away.

The newly composed image was assembled from 24 individual Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 exposures taken in October 1999, January 2000, and December 2000. The colors in the image indicate the different elements that were expelled during the explosion. Blue in the filaments in the outer part of the nebula represents neutral oxygen, green is singly-ionized sulfur, and red indicates doubly-ionized oxygen.

gallery.title: File:Roberta colallillo 06 auger aera.jpg
gallery.description: AERA is a new antenna system to measure short radio pulses emitted by cosmic ray air showers of the highest energies. It consists of an array of dozens of antennas sensitive in the frequency range of 30 to 80 MHz with signal processing and electronics developed specifically for this purpose.

gallery.title: File:Roberta colallillo 05 auger heat.jpg
gallery.description: The High Elevation Auger Telescopes (HEAT) are three tiltable fluorescence telescopes which represent a low energy enhancement of the fluorescence telescope system of the southern site of the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina. The Pierre Auger Observatory is a hybrid cosmic ray detector consisting of 24 fluorescence telescopes to measure the fluorescence light of extensive air showers complemented by 1600 water Cherenkov detectors to determine the particle densities at ground. In this configuration air showers with a primary energy of 10^18 eV and above are investigated. By lowering the energy threshold by approximately one order of magnitude down to a primary energy of 10^17 eV, HEAT provides the possibility to study the cosmic ray energy spectrum and mass composition in a very interesting energy range, where the transition from galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays is expected to happen. The standard fluorescence telescopes have a field of view (FOV) n elevation up to 30°, HEAT telescopes, instead have a 30°-60° FOV. They worked in combination with the standard Coihueco telescopes.

gallery.title: File:Roberta colallillo 12 auger tank.jpg
gallery.description: The Pierre Auger Observatory is a hybrid cosmic ray detector consisting of 24 fluorescence telescopes to measure the fluorescence light of extensive air showers complemented by 1600 water Cherenkov detectors to determine the particle densities at ground. A SD stations consist of a 3.6 m diameter tank containing a sealed liner with a reflective inner surface. This one is filled with 12000 liters of pure water. Shower particles pass through the water and produce Cherenkov light, that is collected by three nine-inch-diameter photomultiplier tubes that are symmetrically distributed at a distance of 1.20 m from the center of the tank and look downwards through windows of clear polyethylene into the water. The station has also a solar power system, which provides an average of 10 Watts for the PMTs, and electronics package consisting of a processor, GPS receiver, radio transceiver and power controller.

gallery.title: File:Roberta colallillo 13 auger coihueco.jpg
gallery.description: Fluorescence detectors (FD) measure the longitudinal profile of an air shower in a calorimetric way. The FD of the Auger Observatory is composed of four observation sites, called `"eyes'". Their names are Los Leones, Los Morados, Loma Amarilla, and Coiheuco. Each eye consists of six independent telescopes. The optical system is composed of a filter at the entrance window of each FD telescope, a circular aperture, a corrector ring, a mirror and a camera with photomultipliers.

gallery.title: File:PierreAugerObservatoryDF-dron.jpg
gallery.description: Aerial view of one of the Pierre Auger Observatory's Fluorescence buildings. Each building houses six mirrors (4x4 meters each), which are part of the fluorescence detectors. The Observatory has four similar buildings and a total of 27 telescopes.

gallery.title: File:PierreAugerObservatory-SD-aligned.jpg
gallery.description: View of the Pierre Auger Observatory's surface detector array. These detectors are arranged in a hexagon array. The detectors are generally spaced 1.5 km apart, and in total (1,660 detectors) cover an area of ​​3,000 square kilometers.taken with a DJI Mavic Pro 1 drone

gallery.title: File:PierreAugerObservaty-LosLeones-DS-FD-LIDAR.jpg
gallery.description: View of the Pierre Auger Observatory near Cerro Los Leones. In the foreground is one of the 1,660 surface detectors (DS), and behind it is the Los Leones fluorescence building (FD) (right), with the communications antenna and atmospheric monitoring LIDAR system (left). The image was acquired with a Sony Alpha 6400 camera.

gallery.title: File:PierreAugerObservatory-PampaAmarilla-DS-scale.jpg
gallery.description: View of one of the surface detectors at the Pierre Auger Observatory. The tanks measure 1.2 m high by 3.6 m in diameter and contain 12,000 liters of ultrapure water. Cherecov radiation is produced when particles in the secondary particle shower generated by the primary cosmic ray pass through the water.The image was taken with a DJI Mavic Pro 1 drone
